records.name: Yemen
records.summary_text:
Yemen is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

records.name: Bhutan
records.summary_text: Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. records.name: Laos
records.summary_text: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans in this country, which has a socially visible tradition of trans-feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation — the one-party system restricts all civil society — and no documented recourse. The tourist cities are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque system) more than violent.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Laos
sources.claim_summary: Homosexuality is legal in Laos. Claims have suggested that Laos is "one of the most tolerant" communist states. A Gallup poll in June 2024 found that Laos was a gay-friendly country and 54% of Laotians thought that their country was a good place to live for gay people.

records.name: Papua New Guinea
records.summary_text:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

records.name: Botswana
records.summary_text: Botswana is workable for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017).
